title: Harness traffic fidelity & script gating scoping
summary: POC scoping to define benchmark success criteria, workload sizing and harness integration approach. Main focus: customer-provided scripts, traffic fidelity (synthetic vs replay), streaming vs non-streaming behavior, KV/cache warmup, acceptance thresholds and 3-week pilot timeline. Agreed next steps: share harness adapter checklist, schedule ingestion test, provide cost/throughput estimate and security docs.
topics: streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs and fallthrough
KV cache warmup strategy and window sizing
traffic fidelity: synthetic vs live replay
action_items: Carlos Reyes: share harness adapter checklist + example adapter repo (due 2026-09-02)
Jordan Patel: upload representative customer scripts and sample logs to shared folder (due 2026-09-03)
Maya Chen: send high-level pilot pricing estimate and capacity guidance (due 2026-09-01)
Aisha Thompson: confirm required data residency/KMS constraints and firewall IPs (due 2026-09-04)
next_steps: Redwood to validate customer scripts with adapter in a small sandbox run
Schedule 90-min integration workshop next week to walk adapter and telemetry hooks
Run initial 2-hour traffic replay to measure cold start and K V cache warmup behavior
Agree on success thresholds and create acceptance spreadsheet
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, um today we want to walk through the harness integration approach and make sure the success criteria for the POC are clear. Jordan, could you start with the use case?
[00:09] Jordan Patel: yeah thanks Maya, so Codexify runs a developer assistance product, mostly short-form completions and a few multi-turn chat flows. We have a mix of interactive features and batch rerank jobs. The critical piece for us is streaming latencies for the dev console — p95 matter a lot because users notice tail.
[00:26] Nina Rao: and to add, we also have offline embedding work for search re-indexing but that can be run in batch out of band. For the POC we'd like to validate both interactive streaming and a separate non-streaming batch path.
[00:39] Carlos Reyes: great, thanks. Quick clarification: when you say streaming do you mean token-streaming to client (SSE/WS) versus chunked HTTP poll?
[00:47] Ben Lowe: token-streaming via websockets is the primary. Some fallbacks will be long-poll for older clients.
[00:54] Carlos Reyes: ok makes sense. So the harness will need to simulate client adapters that expect streaming responses and also the longpoll fallback.
[01:03] Jordan Patel: we're planning to hand you our existing client-side scripts which do replay of production traces. we also have a synthetic generator that bumps up concurrency for stress runs.
[01:13] Maya Chen: perfect — important we get both, because synthetic stresses and faithful replay exercise different hotspots. Replay preserves profile shape (session lengths, token distributions) and synthetic is good for throughput/scale.
[01:25] Aisha Thompson: one thing we care about is KV cache warmup — earlier tests with another vendor showed huge tails until the cache warmed. how do you plan to measure warmup windows?
[01:36] Carlos Reyes: we typically run a staged replay: initial warmup window (10-20 minutes) to populate KV and prefix caches, then a measurement window for steady-state. We'll instrument per-request cache hit metrics and measure cold-start percentiles separately.
[01:48] Nina Rao: can you capture per-session KV hit rate? our flows have long context windows so the effectiveness of the cache is crucial to cost and latency.
[01:56] Carlos Reyes: yes we can surface KV hits per session, token-level counts, and we can export a CSV with per-minute hit rates.
[02:04] Ben Lowe: success criteria — let's call them out now. For streaming interactive we want p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 700ms, and under 3% error rate. For batch embeddings, throughput of 20k embeddings/hour at under $0.01 per embedding is target.
[02:20] Maya Chen: noted. We typically ask for acceptance buckets: functional correctness (no regressions on eval prompt set), latency SLOs, throughput economics, and platform reliability (no more than two incidents during pilot).
[02:33] Jordan Patel: about functional correctness — we have a small eval suite of 500 prompts, we want to ensure model variant changes or quantization don't degrade quality by more than 2% on our metrics.
[02:43] Carlos Reyes: okay we'll run the eval harness in parallel and report regression deltas. We do quantized runs too but we want to keep fidelity checks.
[02:51] Maya Chen: how long is realistic for the pilot? We recommended three weeks historically. Thoughts?
[02:58] Nina Rao: three weeks seems fine: week 1 adapter + sanity and warmup runs, week 2 full replay + tuning, week 3 acceptance and wrap.
[03:07] Aisha Thompson: we also need a security review slot in week 2 for SAML and KMS questions.
[03:14] Carlos Reyes: we'll bring our security checklist. For private deployment constraints we can run either on Redwood Dedicated or Private; you'll tell us which based on your compliance needs.
[03:22] Jordan Patel: we need VPC connectivity and customer KMS for encryption at rest. shared keys are not acceptable.
[03:29] Maya Chen: noted. we'll include the KMS/IP firewall doc in the package.
[03:33] Ben Lowe: One concern: streaming fallthrough if the model variant becomes unavailable — do you have automatic fallback to lower-tier models to preserve availability?
[03:41] Carlos Reyes: yes, we support policy-based routing: route by latency SLOs or cost, and fallback to a compatible variant automatically. We'll include that in the runbook and show behavior in a failover test.
[03:52] Jordan Patel: for the harness adapter: requirements? we have node/python services. prefer python.
[03:58] Carlos Reyes: we have example adapters in Python and Node. We need a light wrapper to format requests the same way your client does (headers, streaming framing). Also an adapter will provide telemetry hooks to emit traces and token timings.
[04:12] Maya Chen: share the adapter checklist after call.
[04:16] [-- 5 minute skip, side channel notes --]
[09:23] Maya Chen: ok back on track. A couple of particulars: traffic fidelity — we want you to provide both replay (sessionized) and synthetic (load spike) scripts. Replay will test correctness and cache patterns. Synthetic tests will stress batch schedulers and autoscale behaviour.
[09:36] Jordan Patel: for replay velocity, we can provide 24 hours of traces that mimic real user concurrency. do you need anonymized tokens or full prompts?
[09:45] Carlos Reyes: anonymized prompts are fine as long as token length distribution and session boundaries are preserved. If there are secret tokens or PII, scrub them — we'll sign an NDA on sample data if needed.
[09:55] Nina Rao: about telemetry — we need per-token latency, model variant labels, KV hit/miss, egress bytes. can your harness capture all of those?
[10:05] Carlos Reyes: yes, our telemetry agent records per-token timing, variant names, and can tag events with adapter session ids. We'll ask you to pass a session-id header.
[10:13] Ben Lowe: for evaluation, we want automated regression diffs against the 500 prompt suite after each config change. is that built in?
[10:20] Carlos Reyes: we can run the eval at end of each major test and produce a delta sheet. we'll also flag any hallucination/regression that exceeds your thresholds.
[10:29] Maya Chen: costs — Jordan asked about cost guides. For pilot we typically provide a cost/throughput estimate. For your target of 20k embeddings/hour and streaming p95 target, initial estimate is X per hour; we'll send a more detailed spreadsheet.
[10:45] Jordan Patel: what's X? can you ballpark now?
[10:48] Maya Chen: ballpark only — depending on model and quantization, expect $X to $Y per 1k tokens; we'll put accurate numbers in the pricing sheet.
[10:57] Aisha Thompson: security loop: we require SOC2 type II evidence and audit logs. Do you provide audit logs per request?
[11:05] Carlos Reyes: Yes we provide audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM. We'll include long retention options as an add-on.
[11:14] Nina Rao: latency SLO verification — we want to see p95 and p99 metrics from both client-side and server-side. Are both captured?
[11:23] Carlos Reyes: yes server-side and client-side; the adapter can measure client-observed times and our runtime traces server-side. We'll correlate them.
[11:30] Ben Lowe: fallback behaviour — what happens to streaming clients when service degrades? do you buffer and flush or drop?
[11:37] Carlos Reyes: by default we try to preserve stream continuity and use backpressure; if model stall occurs beyond threshold we send a structured error and optionally fallback to a synchronous response. We'll demo the failover.
[11:48] Maya Chen: let's talk acceptance gates in more detail. I propose: 1) replay run: p95 <= 350ms for streaming across 90% of sessions; 2) throughput run: hit 2x expected peak concurrency at 80% of estimated cost; 3) regression: no more than 2% degradation on the eval suite. Anyone object?
[12:07] Jordan Patel: sounds good, maybe adjust the 2x to 1.5x for initial safety.
[12:12] Nina Rao: +1 to 1.5x, we want to avoid overshooting for a first-run.
[12:16] Maya Chen: ok we'll set 1.5x.
[12:19] [14:00] Carlos Reyes: about the harness telemetry exports — we'll provide csvs and a prometheus remote write option. Which do you prefer?
[14:07] Jordan Patel: we want csvs for immediate analysis and prometheus for long-term dashboards.
[14:12] Carlos Reyes: got it. We'll enable both.
[14:17] Ben Lowe: timeline recap?
[14:20] Maya Chen: week 0 (this week): share adapter checklist and sample adapters; week 1: integration + warmup runs; week 2: full replay + synthetic stress + security review; week 3: acceptance, regression and handoff. Final sign-off end of week 3.
[14:36] Aisha Thompson: do you need firewall IPs from our side?
[14:39] Carlos Reyes: yes we'll list the IPs and ports. If you're on Private we can do direct peering.
[14:45] Jordan Patel: one more item — client-side framing uses a custom header X-Codexify-Session. we'll include that in adapter mapping.
[14:52] Carlos Reyes: perfect.
[14:55] Maya Chen: ok we're almost done. Any other risks?
[14:59] Nina Rao: data residency still a question — can Dedicated be deployed in our GCP eu-west region?
[15:05] Maya Chen: Dedicated regional capacity yes, we'll confirm availability; if not we'll propose a private node.
[15:12] Ben Lowe: how do you handle version pinning during POC? we can't have the model change mid-run.
[15:18] Carlos Reyes: you can pin model versions and we can snapshot config for the acceptance runs. Any rollout will be separate.
[15:25] Jordan Patel: ok. final note on scripts: we'll send a README with how to run them. expect a 500-1k session file and a synthetic generator that hits 2k concurrent clients for stress runs.
[15:36] Maya Chen: excellent. we'll follow up with a combined runbook and the pricing/ops docs. thanks everyone.
[15:42] Ben Lowe: thanks all.
[15:45] [call ends]
notes: Adapter checklist: https://redwood.example/s/adapter-checklist (placeholder). Customer to upload scripts to shared folder: https://drive.codexify.com/poc/harness. Pricing sheet will be sent as 'POC Pricing - Codexify.xlsx'.
